endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Establish an AI workforce competency framework (or related document) that defines: roles and responsibilities of AI governance personnel, minimum qualifications and/or certification.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is important to identify the parties responsible for data monitoring and note whether they are qualified for those tasks.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Conduct regular monitoring of GAI systems and publish reports detailing the performance, feedback received, and improvements made.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: A description of the users who make configuration decisions (e.g., clinical user, 411 administrative user, patient) including any necessary qualifications and training 412 needed to make these decisions

endorsements.title: Current challenges for global equity related to the implementation of artificial intelligence in pediatric imaging
endorsements.quote: Therefore, protected roles for clinical AI leadership, coupled with investment in multidisciplinary training that includes (pediatric) radiologists, radiographers, physicists, and IT specialists, are crucial for ensuring that AI in pediatric imaging evolves in a manner that is safe, equitable, sustainable, and globally relevant.

commentary.bottom_line: Four of the five endorsing sources, including CHAI playbooks and FDA draft guidance, call for defining roles and qualifications for staff who govern, configure, or monitor AI, while NIST AI 600-1 addresses regular monitoring and reporting rather than staff qualifications. No supplied study tests whether defining or verifying competencies reduces missed failures, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus and regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the evidence set tests competency frameworks or qualification checks for AI roles, and no study documents the hazard itself. Under GRADE conventions, this means there is no direct evidence to rate. The endorsements consist of frameworks, draft guidance, and one commentary, which reflect expert opinion rather than a tested effect.

The targeted failure mode is that unqualified staff miss AI malfunctions before they reach patients. No supplied study measures how often this occurs or whether qualified staff catch more errors. The safeguard is plausible, but its capacity to intercept failures has not been measured in this evidence set.

FDA draft guidance asks manufacturers to describe who makes configuration decisions and the qualifications and training they need. CHAI playbooks state that governance personnel roles and minimum qualifications must be defined. The FDA text is draft and addresses manufacturer submissions, and NIST AI 600-1 speaks to monitoring and reporting rather than personnel qualifications.

One commentary on pediatric imaging calls for protected AI leadership roles and multidisciplinary training to support safe and equitable implementation. It reports no data. No supplied study examines whether staff qualifications affect AI configuration or monitoring in safety-net or Medicaid settings.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI monitoring or configuration outcomes, such as time to detect performance drift, configuration error rates, or patient harm events, between health systems or units that verify staff competencies and those that do not. Studies are also needed to identify which qualifications predict effective AI oversight and what verification costs.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of competency requirements for AI roles in those settings is unknown.
